g.text: System design — session analytics for user activity
two extra stages, a store that must accept deletions, and 5 data-dependent state entries
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
SESSION ANALYTICS — SIX STAGES
the merger and the retraction emitter exist only because boundaries can move
event source
events with event time and a key
window assigner
assigns to a session whose bounds are PROVISIONAL
session merger
the stage fixed and sliding windows do not have
keyed session state
5 entries here — a data-dependent count
trigger / retraction emitter
must be able to un-say a published session
analytics store
must accept a retraction, or the counts drift
Two of these six stages exist solely because a session's bounds can change after the fact: the merger and the retraction emitter.
So "we'll use session windows" is a decision that adds two components and a requirement on the downstream store. It is not a configuration
change.
Step 1/4 — the pipeline, and the stage that only sessions need
Name what sessions cost before designing with them. The merger and the retraction emitter have no equivalent in a fixed-window pipeline, and the
analytics store acquires a hard requirement: it must accept a retraction. A store that can only append is not compatible with session windows at
all, and that is discovered late if it is not named here.
System design — session analytics for user activity
two extra stages, a store that must accept deletions, and 5 data-dependent state entries
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
WHAT THE STORE RECEIVES — key "b", gap 40s
the window identity changes, not just its value
event 4 — session emitted
[12:01:30, 12:01:30] ids 2 sum 7 → store holds 7
event 7 — id 7 arrives (et 12:00:50)
it belongs to that session, which is already published
the emitter must send
store, if it ignores the retraction
18 for a session worth 11 — 64% over
Note the retraction names the OLD BOUNDS. A store keyed by session bounds has a row for [12:01:30, 12:01:30] that must be deleted, not updated —
the new session has a different key.
That is the practical difference from a fixed window's retraction, where the key stays the same and only the value moves.
Step 2/4 — the retraction, with real values
The sharp detail is in the note: a fixed window's correction updates a row, and a session's correction **deletes one row and inserts another**,
because the session's bounds are its identity. A store keyed by (key, session start) cannot express that as an update — and a pipeline that emits
only the new value leaves the old row behind, reading 18 where 11 is right.
System design — session analytics for user activity
two extra stages, a store that must accept deletions, and 5 data-dependent state entries
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
GAP AND ALLOWED LATENESS, TOGETHER
one setting with two consequences, and one that prices the first
gap = 120s (this book)
key a: 3 sessions · 0 retractions needed
gap = 40s
key a: 4 sessions · 1 retraction needed
the gap decides BOTH
how many sessions exist, AND whether retraction is required
allowed lateness decides
how long a collected session can still be revived — i.e. the memory bill
A smaller gap means more sessions AND earlier collection, which is what creates the retraction: the session was closed before its straggler
arrived.
So tightening the gap to get cleaner "visits" silently turns on the requirement that the store accept deletions. The two consequences are not
independent.
Step 3/4 — the two settings that decide the whole design
The coupling in the note is the thing to take away. Shrinking the gap from 120s to 40s changes key a from 3 to 4 sessions — and simultaneously
makes 1 retraction mandatory, because sessions now close before the straggler lands. A product decision about what counts as a visit reaches into
the storage contract.
System design — session analytics for user activity
two extra stages, a store that must accept deletions, and 5 data-dependent state entries
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
SCOPE
Session state is data-dependent: 5 entries for 9 events here, and nothing in this design bounds it for a burstier stream or more keys.
One session is never collected, because the watermark never reaches 12:11:00. Its memory is held for the life of the job regardless of allowed
lateness.
This stream's late event EXTENDS a session. A late event that BRIDGES two already-emitted sessions would require retracting two panes and
emitting one — the same mechanism, twice the bookkeeping, and no event here does it.
And the gap 120s is a definition nobody can verify. Every session count in this chapter is correct for that definition and for no other.
Step 4/4 — and what this design does NOT settle
The third note is worth stating plainly rather than implying: this dataset's straggler extends one session, so the bridge case — one event merging
two already-published sessions — is not demonstrated here. It is the same retraction mechanism applied twice, and a design that handles the
extension handles it, but no number in this chapter proves that.
